docs.title: mib2q plugin SDK
docs.text:
Write plugins for the MIB2 High head unit in modern Java or Kotlin.

The MIB2 High runs a 2008-era IBM J9 Java VM inside a QNX head unit. This SDK gives it a small plugin platform in the spirit of Bukkit or Fabric: you write ordinary Java against a stable API, and the SDK handles class-file backporting, loading, permissions, isolation, UI and recovery.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Getting started

    Install the SDK, create a project from the template, and build your first jar.

  • Tutorial

    Build the coffee-timer plugin step by step: a Car row, a page, a slider and a status item.

  • Project layout

    Learn what lives in a plugin project, what ships to the unit, and where the Java/native boundary is.

  • Java API reference

    Generated documentation for mibsdk.api, the test harness and the fake car.

docs.title: What a plugin can do
docs.text:
• Add a page built from native list cells, checkboxes, sliders, dropdowns and progress rows.
  • Add a row to the Car drawer and a short item to the status line.
  • Show toasts and dialogs using the HMI's own widgets.
  • Run background work with a scheduler, persistent storage and TCP networking: loopback by default, outbound with an extra permission.
  • Read vehicle state and parking-sound changes, and hold an override the SDK restores afterwards.

docs.title: Supported hardware
docs.text:
Unit MHI2Q (MIB2 High, QNX), the unit mibpkg calls MHI2Q HMI build HMI_AU_MIB2_HQC_NAR_G22_C10_180803 Package manager mibpkg 0.9.1 or later Plugin API 1 through 7 (SDK 0.6.2)

The firmware check is strict: on any other HMI build the SDK stays off and loads no plugins.

Experimental software for a car

This SDK has been verified on a bench MHI2Q, not yet on a car. It changes how the stock HMI boots, and a broken install can leave the HMI misbehaving until you recover it. Read the safety model before installing. Installing this software is likely to void your warranty, and nothing here is affiliated with or endorsed by the vehicle or head-unit manufacturers.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The SDK is a small project with a large surface: a Java runtime, a firmware adapter, a Gradle build plugin, a template, a Python installer tool and these docs. Contributions are welcome.

docs.title: Good places to start
docs.text:
• A sample plugin or a plugin recipe that shows a pattern the docs do not cover.
  • A documentation fix: a broken command, a stale limit, a confusing explanation.
  • A test that reproduces a bug on the fake car.
  • A portability fix that keeps the car's Java 1.4 constraints intact.
  • An adapter for another MHI2Q firmware build. Start with Adding a firmware adapter and Stock files.

docs.title: Before you change code
docs.text:
Read Architecture and Safety model. The non-negotiables:

  • plugin code never runs on a stock HMI thread;
  • on-unit classes stay class-file v48;
  • runtime, platform and compat stay Java 1.4 API;
  • API changes are additive;
  • the plugin class loader stays filtered;
  • no stock classes outside adapter-hqc.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open an issue describing the change, or comment on an existing one.
  2. Branch from main.
  3. Make the change and add tests.
  4. Run the gates in Build and test.
  5. Update the docs and CHANGELOG.md in the same change.
  6. Open a pull request.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The docs are built from docs/ with MkDocs Material. The API reference is generated from Javadoc with Dokka. If you change behaviour, update the page that describes it, the reference table that lists it and the Javadoc that contracts it.

The docs style guide explains the voice and structure.

docs.title: Adding a firmware adapter
docs.text:
The plugin API is firmware-neutral. All car-specific code lives in one adapter behind mibsdk.platform.PlatformAdapter. The repository ships one adapter, adapter-hqc, for HMI_AU_MIB2_HQC_NAR_G22_C10_180803.

This page is the investigation and implementation guide for a second adapter. It is deliberately concrete: you will pull files, build a map, and prove each layer on a bench unit before touching a car.

Warning

A wrong adapter can boot-loop the HMI. Work on a bench unit, keep SSH or SD-card recovery available, and test safe mode before you install anything on a car.

docs.title: 1. What an adapter has to provide
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    RT["mibsdk.runtime"] --> SPI["mibsdk.platform.PlatformAdapter"]
    SPI --> V["supports(hmiVersion)"]
    SPI --> F["features()"]
    SPI --> S["start(host) / stop()"]
    SPI --> P["parking()"]
    S --> B["bundle activator / configurator"]
    S --> UI["UI: pages, Car rows, status bar, toasts, dialogs"]
    S --> EV["events: ignition, parking, trailer, hooks"]
SPI member What it must do id() A short adapter name, used in logs supports(hmiVersion) Exact match against the HMI = ... line, or a deliberate family rule features() The mibsdk.api.Features this build can provide start(PlatformHost) Register with the stock HMI, create the UI and event bridges, report features stop() Remove everything; restore stock state parking() A ParkingIo or null when the unit has no parking system

The runtime never sees an stock HMI class. The adapter is the only module allowed to.

docs.title: 2. Inventory the unit
docs.text:
Start with the version and the boot chain.

ssh root@<unit-ip> 'grep "^HMI" /ifs/version_info.txt'
ssh root@<unit-ip> 'ls -la /mnt/app/eso/hmi/lsd /mnt/app/eso/hmi/lsd/jars /ifs'

Pull the stock files (see Stock files):

./gradlew pullStockJars -Punit=<unit-ip> -PwithJars=1 -Pjxe2jarSrc=/path/to/jxe2jar/src
File What it tells you version_info.txt The exact HMI = ... string your supports must match lsd.sh Boot classpath, heap, system properties, bundle list selection, JXE path bundles*.properties Bundle activators and autostart order lsd/jars/*.jar Classes that shadow the JXE; note duplicates and load order lsd.jxe / lsd.jar The HMI itself: ~30k classes hmi.zip Developer-mode HMI classes, when present DSITracer.jar The DSI service tracer the adapter links against

docs.title: Convert and inspect
docs.text:
The commands below use de.<vendor> and de.<framework> as placeholders for the package prefixes in your image. Find the real prefixes with unzip -l first; do not copy the HQC build's names.

PYTHONPATH=/path/to/jxe2jar/src python3 /path/to/jxe2jar/src/jxe2jar.py \
    build/stock/lsd.jxe build/stock/lsd.jar

unzip -l build/stock/lsd.jar | grep -E 'de/<vendor>|de/<framework>|org/dsi' | head
javap -classpath build/stock/lsd.jar -p de.<vendor>.atip.base.Framework

For readable sources, decompile with CFR or Vineflower. Treat the output as a map, not as truth: jxe2jar byte-swaps some numeric constants and can drop InnerClasses attributes. Verify anything you rely on against the class file with javap or at runtime.

docs.title: 3. Build a firmware map
docs.text:
Write down evidence as you go. A table like this is worth more than a memory of a class name:

Question Where to look Record How does the HMI start? lsd.sh, startup.sh, runHMI.sh Command line, JXE path, boot classpath Which bundles start? bundles.properties, bundles_*.properties Activator class, autostart order What wraps DSI? the serviceDelegateConfigurator property, DSITracer.jar Configurator class and chain order Where is the framework? IFrameworkAccess, the framework access class Service name, lookup method Where is the screen model? DisplayManagerMIB2High, HMITerminalImplMIB2High Context ids, terminal ids Where do screens come from? *ScreenFactory, ScreenBag, ConditionBank Factory class, model ids Where is the status bar? StatusBar*, PartialPopup* Widget ids, model ids How does input arrive? KbdListener, KeyEventDistributorEvo Key codes, focus path How is parking exposed? org.dsi.ifc.*parking*, ParkingBridge in HQC Service name, methods

The HQC adapter's classes are the reference for each row:

HQC class Pattern to copy HqcVersion Exact version match SdkBundleActivator Bundle entry point and lifecycle ConfiguratorCore, ChainingConfigurator Hooking the stock configurator chain HqcPlatform PlatformAdapter implementation and feature set SdkBoot, SdkGlobals, SdkFiles Runtime boot and on-unit paths ServiceWaiter, RawServices Waiting for late stock services DsiServiceProxy, DsiConstants, BridgeListener DSI proxies and event pumps IgnitionBridge, ParkingBridge, HookBindings Events, parking and hooks ui/HqcUiIds, ui/TextIds, ui/InputTextIds Stock id tables ui/SdkCarActivator, ui/SdkCarScreenFactory, ui/SdkCarModelBank Car drawer and screens ui/SdkSystemActivator, ui/SdkSystemScreenFactory Plugins menu and status bar ui/PageScreens, ui/PageRenderer, ui/PageWidgets Page rendering ui/BarStatusLine, ui/StatusSinks, ui/StatusPopupController Status-line and popup paths ui/ConfirmScreen, ui/SliderScreen, ui/SpellerScreen Dialogs and inputs ui/UiApplier, ui/UiInputs, ui/HmiPoster Applying snapshots and input

docs.title: How to find a class you only know by behaviour
docs.text:
# Class names, without decompiling everything
unzip -l build/stock/lsd.jar | grep -i statusbar

# A string constant, a log line or a method name in the jar
zipgrep -a 'PDC R OFF' build/stock/lsd.jar || true

# One class's full signature
javap -classpath build/stock/lsd.jar -p -c de.<vendor>.atip.displaymanager.DSIDisplayManagerControllerImpl

# Decompile one package
cfr build/stock/lsd.jar --outputdir build/stock/src --jarfilter 'de.<vendor>.atip.base.*'

Prefer javap for facts and decompilers for shape. A decompiled name is a guess until the bytecode or the bench confirms it.

docs.title: 4. Implement the adapter
docs.text:
1. Copy the module shape. Create adapter-<name> with the same dependencies as adapter-hqc: the stock lsd.jar and DSITracer.jar, platform, and the mibsdk.car-library convention.
  2. Version gate first. Implement supports and make the SDK log adapter=none and stop on an unknown build. Never fall through to an HMI you have not tested.
  3. Boot. Register a bundle activator and a configurator chain. Prove that the SDK starts, logs its STATUS lines and stops cleanly before you add UI.
  4. Services. Wait for the framework access and the DSI services. Report features only when the service is actually available. Handle services that arrive late: call PlatformHost.featuresChanged().
  5. UI, one path at a time: Plugins menu, page, Car row, status item, toast, confirm. Keep the id tables in one class (HqcUiIds is the model) and never scatter raw stock ids.
  6. Events and parking. Prove ignition and parking events, then the override and restore path.
  7. Hooks last. Hooks depend on the DSI proxy and the stock thread model. Prove that no plugin code runs on a stock thread.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not let plugin code touch the manufacturer's stock packages or org.dsi.*. The class-loader allow-list is the boundary.
  • Do not shadow a stock class unless there is no other way. Every shadow is a firmware-specific liability.
  • Do not run plugin code from a stock callback. Queue it on the plugin's worker.
  • Do not assume a screen, model id or key code from another firmware. Measure it.
  • Do not ship a stock jar, a decompiled class or an HMI image.

docs.title: 5. Bench loop
docs.text:
The adapter is the one part that cannot be tested on the host fake. Use a bench unit:

  1. ./gradlew :dist:assembleUnit and ./gradlew :dist:mibpkgPackage.
  2. Install the SDK with installer/mibsdk-dev install <unit-ip>.
  3. Watch installer/mibsdk-dev log <unit-ip> for STATUS lines and startup errors.
  4. Use installer/mibsdk-dev ui-forcefail factory|screen|off to prove the fallback paths.
  5. Capture the screen after every UI change. A screenshot is evidence that the stock HMI drew what you think it did.
  6. Test safe mode: installer/mibsdk-dev safe-mode on, reboot, then off.
  7. Test a plugin that fails in onEnable, one that hangs, and one that is quarantined.

docs.title: Evidence to collect
docs.text: Area Evidence Version gate Unknown build logs adapter=none and loads no plugin Boot Warm and cold boot, no boot loop, clean stop Menu SDK entry, Plugins page, Car drawer row Pages Every row kind and input on the real HMI Status bar Text, icon, colour, contexts, pagination, icon-only Dialogs Confirm, speller, toast, BACK and timeout Parking Read, override, restore on disable and ignition-off Hooks Veto and observe, no plugin code on a stock thread Recovery Safe mode, failed restore retry, uninstall restores stock files

docs.title: 6. Definition of done
docs.text:
• supports matches exactly the documented build; anything else makes the SDK stay off.
  • Every PlatformAdapter method is implemented and tested.
  • Every reported Feature is real at that boot; a missing service is reported as missing.
  • Plugin code never runs on a stock thread.
  • The adapter compiles against the stock jars and passes linkCheck.
  • carJclSignatures is regenerated and committed if the class library changed.
  • A bench record exists for every UI path, with screenshots and a clean log.
  • Safe mode and uninstall are tested.
  • The docs say which build the adapter supports and what is still unproven.

docs.title: 7. Tips for a person or an agent
docs.text:
• Start with the version gate and the boot chain. Do not read 30,000 classes first.
  • Build a map with exact class names, method names and evidence. Update it after every bench run.
  • Use javap to confirm a signature; use a decompiler to understand the shape.
  • Check whether a class is in lsd.jxe or in a shadow jar. The first copy on the boot classpath wins.
  • When a name looks meaningful (StatusBarStubController), verify it with the model id it writes.
  • Keep every experiment on a branch and in the bench record. A second adapter is a long investigation.
  • The repository's internal research notes show the shape of one such map: the onboard Java map and the HMI UI injection notes. They describe the HQC build, not yours, but the questions and evidence style transfer.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 17 (Gradle runs on it).
  • JDK 8 (the toolchain detects or downloads one).
  • The stock lsd.jar and DSITracer.jar for adapter-hqc and dist.
  • Host mibpkg for packaging.
  • Python 3 for the installer and icon tests, and for the docs site.
  • MkDocs Material for the docs site.

A plugin-only checkout does not need the stock jars. The SDK's check does, because it builds the adapter and the distribution.

docs.title: Configure local paths
docs.text:
Put these in $GRADLE_USER_HOME/gradle.properties (by default ~/.gradle/gradle.properties):

mibsdk.stockLsdJar=/path/to/lsd.jar
mibsdk.stockDsiTracerJar=/path/to/DSITracer.jar
mibsdk.mibpkg=/path/to/mibpkg
mibsdk.jdk8Home=/path/to/jdk8        # optional

There are no machine-specific defaults. A missing required property fails with a message naming it. To pull the stock files from a unit, see Stock files.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
./gradlew check
./gradlew :build-logic:test
python3 -m unittest discover -s installer -p 'test_*.py'

check runs:

  • every module's tests;
  • classVersionCheck, linkCheck and permissionScan;
  • build-logic's tests (through the root check);
  • standalonePluginCheck, which scaffolds templates/plugin outside the project graph and builds it against build/repo;
  • carJclSignaturesCheck when mibsdk.stockLsdJar is set.

Reports land in <module>/build/reports/mibsdk/.

docs.title: Common commands
docs.text:
./gradlew :api:test
./gradlew :plugins:coffee-timer:test
./gradlew :plugins:coffee-timer:mibPluginJar
./gradlew publishLocal
./gradlew newPlugin -Pid=my-plugin -Pdir=../my-plugin
./gradlew standalonePluginCheck
./gradlew :dist:assembleUnit
./gradlew :dist:mibpkgPackage
./gradlew carJclSignatures          # needs mibsdk.stockLsdJar
./gradlew pullStockJars -Punit=<unit-ip>   # copies the stock files off a unit

The plugins/ projects are samples, built as subprojects of this build. A standalone plugin uses the same task names without the :plugins:<id>: prefix.

docs.text: Module Notes api Plugin API. Additive changes only; @since api N tags are checked compat Java 1.4 source shims. No generics platform Adapter SPI and UI model runtime Loader, permissions, scheduler, UI, boot guard, ledger adapter-hqc Firmware adapter. docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
python3 -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
./gradlew docsApi                  # Dokka HTML into build/docs-api
./gradlew docsSite                 # MkDocs into build/docs-site, with API and Maven repo
mkdocs serve                       # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000

The docsSite task:

  1. generates the Dokka API reference;
  2. builds the MkDocs site with --strict;
  3. copies Dokka into build/docs-site/api/;
  4. copies build/repo into build/docs-site/maven/ when it exists.

tools/check_docs.py verifies code blocks marked <!-- file: ... --> against the sample files and checks the documented versions against source.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• Java source in api, runtime, platform, compat and adapter-* stays Java 1.4 compatible except where a module explicitly compiles with a newer release.
  • Keep the plugin class loader allow-list and the build's Toolchain.ALLOWED_PARENT_PREFIXES in sync.
  • Add a test for every new runtime state, permission or UI path.
  • Do not add a dependency to the on-unit jars unless it is backported and link-checked.

docs.title: Documentation style guide
docs.text: The docs are for plugin authors first and SDK contributors second. They are not an engineering log.

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Write in the second person: you write a plugin, you install it.
  • Use the active voice and the present tense: "The SDK loads the jar", not "the jar is loaded".
  • Prefer short sentences and short paragraphs. One idea per paragraph.
  • Explain why only when it changes what the reader should do. Otherwise show the code.
  • Do not address an AI, an agent or a future maintainer. Public pages talk to the reader.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Every page should answer one question and fit in one sitting.

  • A page starts with a one-sentence summary of what the reader will do or learn.
  • Prerequisites go near the top, in a short list.
  • Put a runnable command or code sample before the long explanation.
  • End with a "Next" or "Related" link, not a summary of the page.
  • Move exact limits, field lists and tables to Reference. Guides explain the shape; reference pages state the rules.

Choose the page type deliberately:

Type Use it for Tutorial A first, complete success. Numbered steps, no optional branches. Guide A task an experienced reader dips into: "add a slider", "poll a daemon". Reference Exact names, fields, defaults, limits and errors. Explanation Architecture, trade-offs and why the SDK behaves the way it does.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• Every command must run as written from the stated directory.
  • Every code block must be complete enough to paste into the project being described.
  • Use sh for shell blocks and label other languages.
  • Never invent a task name or an API call. Check it against build-logic/ or api/.
  • Tutorial code blocks that mirror a sample use a <!-- file: path --> marker. The docs check compares the block with the file, so the sample and the page cannot drift apart.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
• Use Material for MkDocs admonitions: note, tip, warning, danger, example.
  • Use tables for reference data, not for prose.
  • Use Mermaid for flows and architecture diagrams, and give the diagram alt text.
  • Use repo-relative links for files in this repository, and full URLs for the published pages.

docs.title: What not to write
docs.text:
• Internal names: "the owner", "the bench unit", ticket numbers, plan task numbers, internal directory names.
  • Machine-specific paths or IP addresses.
  • Personal data: VIN, IMSI, location, names, home directory paths.
  • Statements about the future as if they were shipped. Mark experiments and unshipped work.
  • A wall of API surface on a getting-started page. Link to the reference instead.

docs.title: Word budgets
docs.text: Page Target README.md under 1,000 words Getting-started page 300–700 words, plus code Tutorial under 5,000 words Guide under 1,500 words Reference page as long as the facts need, with tables

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Version Where Meaning SDK version mibsdk.version in gradle.properties The mibsdk mibpkg package and Maven artifacts Plugin API api in plugin.json; SdkInfo.API_VERSION The newest API level the SDK implements Plugin version version in a plugin's plugin.json The plugin package version Template version templates/plugin/build.gradle.kts Must equal mibsdk.version

The SDK follows semver. Bench builds may carry a +bench.N tag, but they are not releases.

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text:
1. Bump mibsdk.version in gradle.properties.
  2. Bump the template to the same version in templates/plugin/build.gradle.kts. standalonePluginCheck fails if they differ.
  3. Add a CHANGELOG entry in Keep a Changelog style. Include SDK changes and plugin API changes.
  4. Update the API level table if SdkInfo.API_VERSION changed. ApiLevelsTest checks @since tags.
  5. Update the docs that name the version or a limit.
  6. Run the gates:
./gradlew check
./gradlew :build-logic:test
python3 -m unittest discover -s installer -p 'test_*.py'
python3 tools/check_docs.py
./gradlew docsSite
  1. Publish the artifacts:
./gradlew publishLocal
  1. Tag and push:
git tag v0.6.0
git push origin main --tags

docs.title: What the tag publishes
docs.text:
The docs workflow builds the site, the Dokka API reference and the Maven repository, then deploys them to the gh-pages branch. GitHub Pages must be configured to serve that branch.

  • the documentation site at /;
  • the Dokka API reference at /api/;
  • the Maven repository at /maven/.

The Maven repository contains dev.complex256.mibsdk:api, compat, platform, runtime, adapter-fake, plugin-test, the mibsdk.plugin and mibsdk.car-library Gradle plugins, and their markers. A plugin resolves them from:

https://complex256.github.io/mib2q-plugin-sdk/maven

Released versions are immutable. Do not republish a version that already exists on Pages.

docs.title: The SDK package
docs.text:
dist/build/dist/mibsdk-<version>.mpk needs the unit's stock jars, which are not in CI. Build it locally and attach it to the GitHub release:

./gradlew :dist:mibpkgPackage

The plugin artifacts do not need the stock jars and are published by CI.

docs.title: API changes
docs.text:
• Additive only. A newer SDK runs every older plugin unchanged.
  • Every new public member gets @since api N.
  • ApiLevels in build-logic must know the member, or permissionScan cannot enforce the declared level.
  • SdkInfo.API_VERSION and MIN_API_VERSION move only with a documented compatibility decision.
  • A new API level needs tests for the new members and a docs update.

docs.title: Hotfixes
docs.text: A hotfix is a patch release: bump the patch version, add a CHANGELOG entry, run the gates, tag. If the fix changes plugin behaviour, update the relevant guide and reference page in the same commit.

docs.title: Stock files for an SDK build
docs.text:
A plugin build does not need any stock HMI files. linkCheck uses a committed signature list of the car's class library. You only need the stock jars to build the SDK's firmware adapter (adapter-hqc) and the distribution (dist), or to regenerate the signature list.

The files are the manufacturer's. Never commit them, attach them to a release, or put them in a container image.

docs.title: Pull them from a unit
docs.text:
With SSH access to a unit:

./gradlew pullStockJars -Punit=<unit-ip>

The task runs tools/pull-stock-jars.sh, which copies:

File From Why lsd.jxe /ifs/lsd.jxe The HMI's class image; jxe2jar turns it into lsd.jar DSITracer.jar /mnt/app/eso/hmi/lsd/DSITracer.jar The DSI tracer the adapter links against version_info.txt /ifs/version_info.txt The HMI = ... line the adapter matches

Add -PwithJars=1 to also copy /mnt/app/eso/hmi/lsd/jars/*.jar. These are the boot jars that shadow some classes; they are useful when investigating a new firmware.

The files land in build/stock/. The script writes a build/stock/gradle.properties with the two paths. Add it to your Gradle user home, or pass the properties on the command line:

cat build/stock/gradle.properties >> "${GRADLE_USER_HOME:-$HOME/.gradle}/gradle.properties"

docs.title: Convert lsd.jxe
docs.text:
The SDK needs lsd.jar, an ordinary jar. Use jxe2jar:

git clone https://github.com/luka-dev/jxe2jar
python3 -m pip install bitstring==3.1.9

Then let the task convert it:

./gradlew pullStockJars -Punit=<unit-ip> -Pjxe2jarSrc=/path/to/jxe2jar/src

Or convert by hand:

PYTHONPATH=/path/to/jxe2jar/src python3 /path/to/jxe2jar/src/jxe2jar.py \
    build/stock/lsd.jxe build/stock/lsd.jar

A conversion writes about 30,000 classes and takes a minute or two. The output has known quirks: some numeric constants are byte-swapped, and InnerClasses attributes can be missing. That is fine for linking; it matters when decompiling.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
./gradlew :adapter-hqc:compileJava :dist:assembleUnit

If a property is missing, the build names it:

mibsdk: mibsdk.stockLsdJar is not set
  jxe2jar's lsd.jar (the HMI's class library)
  Set it with -Pmibsdk.stockLsdJar=<path> or in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties; see README.md#toolchain

docs.title: Regenerate the signature list
docs.text:
After changing the supported firmware or the stock files:

./gradlew carJclSignatures -Pmibsdk.stockLsdJar=build/stock/lsd.jar
./gradlew carJclSignaturesCheck

The first writes build-logic/src/main/resources/mibsdk/build/carjcl.sigs; commit that file. It contains class names, supertypes, member names and descriptors only — no bytecode.

docs.title: SSH notes
docs.text:
The unit uses an old RSA host key. The script passes the same options as mibsdk-dev:

-o HostKeyAlgorithms=ssh-rsa -o PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes=ssh-rsa
-o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=8

It logs in as root. Key-based auth must already work. If the unit is not reachable, check the address, the network and ssh root@<unit-ip> by hand.

docs.title: Legal
docs.text: The stock files are proprietary. Keep them on your machine, out of git, out of CI artifacts, and out of anything you publish. The repository's .gitignore already excludes build/.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The SDK exists to make one firmware's HMI programmable without letting a plugin take the unit down. That goal explains nearly every design choice: a narrow API, a filtered class loader, one worker per plugin, declarative hooks and a firmware adapter.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph plugin["Plugin (your code)"]
        P["Java, class-file v48"]
    end
    subgraph sdk["SDK"]
        API["mibsdk.api<br/>stable, firmware-neutral"]
        RT["mibsdk.runtime<br/>loader, lifecycle, permissions, UI"]
        SPI["mibsdk.platform<br/>adapter SPI"]
        AD["adapter-hqc<br/>firmware-specific"]
    end
    subgraph stock["Stock HMI"]
        LSD["lsd.jar on IBM J9 2.3"]
        DSI["DSI services"]
        JNI["JNI / native"]
    end
    P --> API --> RT --> SPI --> AD --> LSD
    LSD --> DSI --> JNI
Layer Responsibility Sees stock classes? Plugin Your feature No mibsdk.api The contract No mibsdk.runtime Discovery, enable/disable, permissions, storage, scheduler, UI table, boot guard No mibsdk.platform The adapter contract and UI snapshot model No adapter-hqc Bundle activator, configurator chain, DSI bridges, HMI drawing Yes Stock HMI The manufacturer's classes, J9, DSI —

A plugin is compiled against mibsdk.api only. The class loader it runs in exposes java.*, javax.*, mibsdk.api.*, mibsdk.compat.* and the Retrotranslator runtime; everything else is hidden. That is why a plugin cannot call a stock HMI class even by accident.

docs.title: Boot
docs.text:
1. lsd.sh puts the SDK jars on the boot classpath.
  2. The SDK bundle activator starts.
  3. The configurator checks /ifs/version_info.txt and selects an adapter. No matching adapter means the SDK stops and loads no plugins.
  4. The BootGuard reads boot.state. If the previous boots were unhealthy, this is a safe-mode boot: pending overrides are restored and no plugins load.
  5. After the configured delay (30 s by default), the runtime discovers plugins/*.jar, validates each plugin.json, checks grants and enables the plugins in dependency order.
  6. healthyAfterMs (60 s) after loading, the boot is marked healthy.
sequenceDiagram
    participant Boot as HMI boot
    participant Guard as BootGuard
    participant RT as Runtime
    participant Plugin
    Boot->>Guard: read boot.state
    alt safe mode
        Guard-->>RT: no plugins
        RT->>RT: restore pending overrides
    else normal
        Guard-->>RT: continue
        RT->>RT: discover and validate jars
        RT->>Plugin: onEnable(ctx) on worker
        RT->>Guard: mark healthy after 60 s
    end

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> DISCOVERED
    DISCOVERED --> BLOCKED_INVALID: bad jar/manifest
    DISCOVERED --> BLOCKED_PERMISSIONS: grant missing
    DISCOVERED --> BLOCKED_DEPENDENCY: dependency not enabled
    DISCOVERED --> ENABLED: onEnable returns
    DISCOVERED --> FAILED: load/onEnable throws
    ENABLED --> QUARANTINED: 3 failures/60s or 30s hang
    ENABLED --> DISABLED: user/reload/stop
    QUARANTINED --> DISABLED
    DISABLED --> ENABLED: re-enable/reload
    FAILED --> DISABLED

Disabling always cancels registrations, releases overrides, flushes storage and then runs onDisable(). A plugin is constructed fresh for each run, so fields do not survive a reload; persistent state belongs in storage.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
Thread Runs HMI dispatcher and stock threads Never plugin code Runtime control thread Load, enable, disable, reload, quarantine One worker per plugin onEnable, onDisable, actions, timers, events, dialog answers Ledger thread Applying and restoring overrides Dev-channel thread Reload markers and log mirroring

One worker per plugin gives plugins a simple concurrency model: callbacks never overlap, so shared fields need no locks. It also means a slow callback delays that plugin only. The worker is a daemon at NORM_PRIORITY - 1.

docs.title: UI
docs.text:
Plugins describe UI; the runtime and adapter draw it.

  1. A plugin builds a PageSpec and calls ui.page.
  2. The runtime stores the page in a UiTable snapshot.
  3. The adapter reads the snapshot and builds stock HMI widgets or list cells.
  4. Input comes back as a UiInput, is mapped to a UiAction, and is queued on the plugin's worker.
  5. Missing features produce inert handles rather than exceptions.

The same UiTable is used by the fake car, which is why host tests exercise the real UI model without the HMI.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions are declared in the manifest, approved by the user and enforced at the API boundary. The build scans code for known permissioned calls; the runtime refuses a call whose permission is not granted. A plugin missing any declared permission does not start.

This is a seat belt, not a sandbox. platform.unrestricted is the explicit escape hatch, and the SDK cannot contain a plugin that uses it.

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
Vehicle writes go through an OverrideLedger:

  • only one plugin may hold an override;
  • the ledger records the prior value in ledger.properties;
  • it restores on disable, uninstall, UNTIL_IGNITION_OFF and safe-mode boot;
  • a failed restore is retried with backoff.

That is why a plugin can mute parking tones without leaving the car muted after a crash.

docs.title: The Java/native boundary
docs.text:
Everything above adapter-hqc is Java. adapter-hqc is also Java, but compiled against the stock jars and allowed to use stock HMI classes. Below it, the stock HMI talks to DSI services and native code (ealswig, Kanzi, the parking ECU) through JNI.

A plugin cannot cross that boundary directly. It reaches native daemons over TCP with ctx.net() (loopback by default, outbound with network.outbound), and stock behaviour through declarative hooks. This keeps plugins portable across firmware adapters and keeps a plugin from depending on a native ABI that may change.

docs.title: Why the build is unusual
docs.text:
The car loads only v48 class files and has a Java 1.4 library. The build therefore:

  1. compiles with JDK 17 and --release 8;
  2. lowers syntax with Retrolambda and Retrotranslator;
  3. checks every class is v48;
  4. checks every reference against a signature list of the car's class library;
  5. checks permissions, API level and forbidden constructs;
  6. stamps the jar so mibpkg can verify it.

A plugin developer sees ordinary Gradle tasks. The unusual parts are hidden behind mibsdk.plugin.

docs.title: The supported build
docs.text:
Unit MHI2Q (MIB2 High, QNX 6.5) HMI build HMI_AU_MIB2_HQC_NAR_G22_C10_180803 Variant FMQ-P-TNSL-US-AU-MLE How it is matched The HMI = ... line of /ifs/version_info.txt, compared exactly

The check is strict. On any other build the SDK finds no matching adapter and stays off; no plugin loads. The SDK package's own manifest also names that build and the MHI2Q unit, so mibpkg refuses to install it elsewhere.

docs.title: Why so strict
docs.text:
The adapter does not sit on a stable public API. It:

  • starts a bundle through the stock 3SOFT OSGi kernel;
  • installs a TraceConfigurator to wrap DSI services;
  • shadows a few stock classes;
  • looks up framework services by name and builds stock widgets;
  • depends on the exact menu, status-bar, icon and DSI behaviour of one HMI build.

A different build moves classes, changes service names, changes screen factories and changes the status bar. Running anyway would be guesswork, and the failure mode is a boot loop.

docs.title: Other units
docs.text:
These are not supported:

  • other MHI2 High builds (different regions, newer software);
  • the non-Q MIB2 High;
  • MIB2 Standard, MIB3, PCM, other vehicle platforms;
  • other vehicle platforms.

Each needs a new firmware adapter. The plugin API is firmware-neutral; the adapter is the only layer that knows a car.

docs.title: What a second adapter would need
docs.text:
1. A map of the HMI's Java: how it boots, how bundles are registered, which services it exposes.
  2. A bundle activator and configurator chain for that build.
  3. A version check for that build.
  4. DSI/parking bridges and the UI implementation: Pages, Car rows, status line, toasts, dialogs, icons.
  5. Bench evidence for every UI path and the parking override.
  6. A package manifest that names the supported build.

The existing adapter is the reference implementation. It is intentionally the only module that touches the manufacturer's stock packages and org.dsi.*.

The full investigation and implementation guide is Adding a firmware adapter. In short:

  1. Read /ifs/version_info.txt and lsd.sh.
  2. Pull lsd.jxe, DSITracer.jar and the boot jars; convert the JXE with jxe2jar.
  3. Build a map of the launch chain, bundles, DSI services, screen factories, status bar and input.
  4. Copy the adapter-hqc module shape and implement PlatformAdapter in stages.
  5. Prove every path on a bench unit before a car.

Do not guess ids, class names or service names from another firmware. The adapter guide lists the exact classes to read, the commands to use, and the evidence to collect.

docs.title: Compatibility with other mods
docs.text: The SDK replaces some stock classes and boot configuration. mibpkg refuses to install it while a third-party mod that shadows the same classes is installed. Other mods that shadow stock classes may conflict for the same reason.

docs.title: Checking a unit
docs.text:
Read the HMI line:

grep '^HMI = ' /ifs/version_info.txt

If it is not exactly the supported build, stop. The SDK will not run.

docs.title: Safety model
docs.text: The SDK is designed so a faulty plugin can break itself but not the head unit's boot, and so a plugin never blocks a stock HMI thread. It is not a security sandbox.

docs.title: 1. Plugin code runs only on its own worker
docs.text:
Each plugin gets one daemon worker thread. onEnable, onDisable, page actions, scheduler tasks, event listeners and dialog answers all run there, one at a time.

Plugin code never runs on:

  • the HMI event dispatcher;
  • a stock service thread;
  • the runtime's control, timer or watchdog thread.

A slow plugin delays its own callbacks, not the HMI.

docs.title: 2. Failures are counted, hangs are cut off
docs.text:
Condition Result A callback throws once Logged; the plugin keeps running 3 callback failures in 60 s Plugin quarantined A callback runs longer than 30 s Plugin quarantined as hung A callback runs longer than 5 s Logged as slow

Lifecycle hooks are special: a throwing onEnable disables the plugin as FAILED immediately; a throwing onDisable is only logged. onDisable still runs after a failed onEnable, so guard your fields.

Quarantine is a disable: registrations are cancelled, overrides released, UI removed and onDisable runs if possible. The plugin stays quarantined until the user re-enables it or the unit restarts. Its code is not rerun to test recovery.

docs.title: 3. Safe mode
docs.text:
If the HMI fails to come up healthy — 60 s without a crash — three boots in a row with plugins enabled, the next boot runs in safe mode:

  • the adapter starts;
  • pending vehicle overrides are restored;
  • no plugin is discovered or loaded, not even by a reload;
  • the Plugins menu reads Plugins (safe mode).

A boot where every plugin FAILED is not counted as unhealthy: a failed plugin runs no code, so a later HMI crash is not its doing.

docs.title: 4. Overrides are restored
docs.text: Vehicle writes go through a ledger. It records the prior value and restores it when the plugin is disabled, quarantined, uninstalled, or the ignition goes off (for UNTIL_IGNITION_OFF). A failed restore is retried with backoff and on the next parking observation or ignition change. On boot, stale entries from a run that ended badly are restored before plugins load.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions are a seat belt:

  • the user sees what a plugin wants before installing it;
  • a plugin missing any declared permission does not run;
  • revoking one stops the plugin;
  • the build refuses known permissioned calls that are not declared.

Outbound network access is a separate permission (network.outbound). It can send data off the unit; approve it only for a plugin you trust.

They do not stop a plugin that sets out to do harm. platform.unrestricted lifts the SDK's build-time and class-loader limits entirely, and mibpkg shows a danger warning. Install only plugins whose source you trust.

docs.title: The heap is small
docs.text: The whole HMI runs with a 60 MB heap. When free heap stays low, the SDK quarantines the most recently enabled plugin. Keep data small; do not cache large strings, images or logs.

docs.title: What the SDK does not protect against
docs.text:
• A plugin with platform.unrestricted can do anything the JVM can.
  • A plugin can start its own thread; the SDK cannot cancel or quarantine it. Do not.
  • A plugin can loop inside a callback until the 30 s hang threshold, delaying itself and its own UI.
  • A bug in the adapter or the runtime is not contained by the plugin model.
  • Firmware updates and other mods can change the assumptions the SDK relies on.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
If the HMI misbehaves after installing a plugin:

  1. Let it boot into safe mode (three unhealthy boots), or force it: installer/mibsdk-dev safe-mode on <unit-ip>.
  2. Remove the plugin: installer/mibsdk-dev remove <id> <unit-ip>.
  3. Uninstall the SDK if needed; it restores the stock files.
  4. Read the log from the failing boot.

Always keep a way to reach the unit (SSH or SD-card recovery) before installing experimental software.

docs.text:
This section takes you from a blank machine to a plugin running on the head unit. Read the pages in order the first time; later, use the guides and reference as needed.

  • Create a plugin

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
The examples use SDK 0.6.2. If you already have a working unit and a JDK:

git clone https://github.com/complex256/mib2q-plugin-sdk.git
cp -R mib2q-plugin-sdk/templates/plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin
./gradlew test
./gradlew mibPluginJar

That produces build/mibsdk/my-plugin.jar. Install the SDK package on the unit once, then install your plugin as a package (.mpk) or push the jar during development. See Install and debug.

docs.title: Before you install anything
docs.text: This is experimental software for a car. Read the safety model first. The SDK has been verified on a bench unit, not yet on a car, and installing it is likely to void your warranty.

docs.title: Create a plugin
docs.text: A plugin is its own Gradle project. It compiles against mibsdk.api from the published Maven repository and is packaged into a .mpk; it does not need a checkout of this SDK.

docs.title: Option 1: copy the template
docs.text:
The fastest route is the standalone template:

git clone https://github.com/complex256/mib2q-plugin-sdk.git
cp -R mib2q-plugin-sdk/templates/plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin

Rename the plugin in three places:

File Change src/main/resources/plugin.json id, name, main, permissions src/main/java/example/myplugin/MyPlugin.java package and class name src/test/java/example/myplugin/MyPluginTest.java package and class name

Then build it:

./gradlew test
./gradlew mibPluginJar

You should see BUILD SUCCESSFUL and build/mibsdk/my-plugin.jar.

docs.title: Option 2: scaffold with newPlugin
docs.text:
From a checkout of the SDK, newPlugin copies the template and rewrites the id, package and class name:

./gradlew newPlugin -Pid=coffee-timer -Pdir=../coffee-timer -Ppackage=tutorial.coffeetimer
Property Meaning -Pid The plugin id in plugin.json. Two to forty characters from a-z, 0-9 and -, starting with a letter. mibsdk is reserved -Pdir Destination directory. It must not exist, or must be empty -Ppackage Java package. Defaults to plugin.<id without dashes>

The task also writes mibsdk.repo in gradle.properties, pointing at the checkout's build/repo, so run ./gradlew publishLocal in the SDK checkout first if you use this route.

docs.title: Option 3: write the files yourself
docs.text:
A plugin is small. The minimum is a build file, a settings file, a manifest and a class.

my-plugin/
├── build.gradle.kts
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── gradle.properties
├── gradlew
├── gradlew.bat
├── gradle/wrapper/
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/example/myplugin/MyPlugin.java
    │   └── resources/plugin.json
    └── test/java/example/myplugin/MyPluginTest.java

docs.title: build.gradle.kts
docs.text:
plugins {
    id("mibsdk.plugin") version "0.6.2"
}

That is the whole build file. The convention compiles, backports, checks, tests and packages the plugin.

docs.title: settings.gradle.kts
docs.text:
pluginManagement {
    repositories {
        val sdkRepo = providers.gradleProperty("mibsdk.repo").orNull?.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }
            ?: "https://complex256.github.io/mib2q-plugin-sdk/maven"
        maven { url = uri(sdkRepo) }
        gradlePluginPortal()
    }
}

dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        val sdkRepo = providers.gradleProperty("mibsdk.repo").orNull?.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }
            ?: "https://complex256.github.io/mib2q-plugin-sdk/maven"
        maven { url = uri(sdkRepo) }
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

plugins {
    id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") version "0.8.0"
}

rootProject.name = "my-plugin"

docs.title: src/main/resources/plugin.json
docs.text:
{
  "id": "my-plugin",
  "name": "My Plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "Your Name",
  "api": 1,
  "main": "example.myplugin.MyPlugin",
  "permissions": []
}

docs.title: src/main/java/example/myplugin/MyPlugin.java
docs.text:
package example.myplugin;

import mibsdk.api.MibPlugin;
import mibsdk.api.PluginContext;

public class MyPlugin extends MibPlugin {
    @Override
    protected void onEnable(PluginContext ctx) {
        ctx.log().info("my-plugin enabled");
    }
}

docs.title: What happens when you build
docs.text:
./gradlew mibPluginJar runs:

  1. compileJava with JDK 17 and --release 8; Jabel accepts newer syntax.
  2. backport to class-file version 48 (Java 1.4) with Retrolambda and Retrotranslator.
  3. classVersionCheck: every class is v48.
  4. linkCheck: every reference resolves against the car's class library.
  5. permissionScan: no reflection or exec without platform.unrestricted, no undeclared permission, no API newer than the "api" you declared.
  6. mibPluginJar: the checked classes plus plugin.json in build/mibsdk/<id>.jar, with a <id>.jar.stamp that records the checks and the SHA-256.

./gradlew test builds the jar first and runs your host tests against the real runtime and a fake car.

docs.title: Package the plugin
docs.text:
./gradlew mibpkgPackage -Pmibsdk.mibpkg=/path/to/mibpkg

The output is build/mibsdk/<id>-<version>.mpk. It contains the stamped jar, your icons, their generated reflections and a manifest.toml that mibpkg reads. Inspect the staged files in build/mibpkg-stage/ if a package looks wrong.

A plugin with "api": 6 needs SDK 0.4.x. mibpkg refuses it on an older SDK.

docs.title: Install the package
The fast development loop
docs.text:
After the package is installed once, push only the jar:

./gradlew mibPluginJar
installer/mibsdk-dev push build/mibsdk/coffee-timer.jar <unit-ip>

The runtime hot-reloads it within a couple of seconds. A push carries no icons and no new permissions:

  • a new icon needs a new package;
  • a new permission needs installer/mibsdk-dev grant <id> <perm,...> <unit-ip>, and the manifest must declare it.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
ctx.log().info/warn/error writes to an in-memory ring buffer. The runtime mirrors it to /tmp/mibsdk.log on the unit:

installer/mibsdk-dev log <unit-ip>

The log also contains the SDK's own STATUS lines, for example:

STATUS coffee-timer FAILED mibsdk.runtime.UndeclaredPermissionException: permission not declared in plugin.json: ui.slot.carmenu at ...

In a host test, h.log() returns the same lines and h.await prints them when a test fails.

docs.title: Plugin states
docs.text: State Meaning What to do ENABLED Running BLOCKED_INVALID Unreadable jar, invalid plugin.json, or the jar is not named <id>.jar Rebuild with mibPluginJar BLOCKED_PERMISSIONS A declared permission is not granted; permissions are all or nothing Approve or grant the full list BLOCKED_DEPENDENCY A declared dependency is missing, blocked, disabled or in a cycle Fix the dependency FAILED Loading the class or onEnable threw; the reason is in the log Fix and push QUARANTINED Three callback failures in 60 s, or one callback hung for 30 s Fix and push; a push or reload starts it again DISABLED Switched off in the Plugins menu or by a reload

docs.title: Quarantine and safe mode
docs.text:
Every callback runs inside a catch-all. One exception is logged and the plugin keeps running. The third within a minute quarantines it: it is disabled, its registrations are cancelled and the Plugins menu says why. A callback still running after 30 s quarantines it as hung. The crashy sample does this on purpose if you want to watch it.

If the HMI fails to come up healthy (60 s without a crash) three boots in a row with plugins enabled, the next boot is in safe mode: the SDK runs with no plugins, restores pending vehicle overrides, and the Plugins menu reads Plugins (safe mode).

installer/mibsdk-dev safe-mode on <unit-ip>     # force it while debugging
installer/mibsdk-dev safe-mode off <unit-ip>    # leave it and reset the boot counter

docs.title: Common failures
docs.text:
permission not declared in plugin.json: X

Your code used something that needs X but the manifest does not list it. Add it and rebuild. The build catches this for known calls, so it is rare on the unit. Granting it on the unit does not help: an undeclared permission can never be used.

permission not granted: X

The manifest declares X but the user has not approved it. Reinstall with approval or run mibsdk-dev grant <id> X <unit-ip>. Normally such a plugin is BLOCKED_PERMISSIONS before it gets far enough to throw this.

a status icon is at most 20x20 px, this one is 72x72

You passed the Car-row icon to statusItem or toast. Ship a 20 px icon and use it there.

icon 'cup' is not declared in plugin coffee-timer's plugin.json "icons"

Add the name to "icons" and make sure src/main/icons/<name>.png exists.

A blank row icon after push

Icons only arrive with a package. Reinstall the .mpk.

A toggle that does not stick

You did not call page.update(spec()) with the new state.

Build failures

linkCheck and permissionScan name the method that made the call. Start at the method they name. See Troubleshooting for the full list.

docs.title: There is no debugger
docs.text: JDWP is disabled on the unit and there is no emulator. Test on the host first. On the unit, use the log, mibsdk-dev status, and safe mode.

docs.title: Install the SDK
docs.text: The SDK is a mibpkg package named mibsdk. Install it once per unit. Plugins are separate packages and can be installed, updated and removed without reinstalling the SDK.

docs.title: Get the package
docs.text:
The package is dist/build/dist/mibsdk-<version>.mpk inside an SDK checkout:

./gradlew :dist:mibpkgPackage

This build needs the stock lsd.jar and DSITracer.jar, which cannot be distributed with the SDK. See Building the SDK if you need to produce the package yourself. If a release asset is published for your version, use that instead.

docs.title: Install it
What the installer changes
docs.text:
All changes are on the writable app partition; no IFS reflash is needed.

  • Adds the three SDK jars: mibsdk-runtime.jar, mibsdk-adapter-hqc.jar and mibsdk-rt-retrotranslator.jar.
  • Adds the permission catalog.
  • Adds a bundle and a DSITracer configurator.
  • Adds the HMICar= and HMISystem= lines the HMI reads.
  • Writes grants.properties for plugin permissions.

Uninstalling the package restores the stock files byte for byte. It does not delete plugin data unless you ask it to.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
1. Restart the HMI or wait for the next boot.
  2. Open MENU → Plugins. You should see the Plugins page with an SDK entry.
  3. If the SDK could not initialise, the page header says Plugins (safe mode) and no plugin runs. Check /tmp/mibsdk.log or run installer/mibsdk-dev log <unit-ip>.

The SDK starts loading plugins 30 seconds after boot by default. A jar installed or pushed later loads within a few seconds.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
installer/mibsdk-dev uninstall <unit-ip>            # keep plugin data
installer/mibsdk-dev uninstall --purge <unit-ip>    # remove plugin data too

Before uninstalling, make sure no plugin holds a vehicle override. --force exists for the case where one does, but the stock value should be restored first.

Any JDK 17 works JDK 8 Retrolambda, Retrotranslator, ProGuard and the Java 1.4 compile The Gradle toolchain. An installed JDK 8 is detected; the foojay resolver downloads one if needed. Override with -Pmibsdk.jdk8Home=<home> Gradle The build The wrapper in the template (./gradlew). docs.text:
Need Why An MHI2Q on HMI build HMI_AU_MIB2_HQC_NAR_G22_C10_180803 The only build with an adapter mibpkg 0.9.1 or later on the unit Package installation and the mibpkg sdk verbs A way to reach the unit mibpkg's web interface, the SD card, or SSH bash and ssh on your computer For the optional installer/mibsdk-dev bench tool

The unit's SSH server uses an old RSA host key. mibsdk-dev passes the right options for you.

Phone-projection mods

mibpkg refuses to install the SDK while a third-party phone-projection mod that shadows the same stock classes is installed.

docs.title: Where the SDK artifacts come from
docs.text:
A plugin resolves dev.complex256.mibsdk:api, compat, plugin-test and the mibsdk.plugin Gradle plugin from a Maven repository. The template uses the published repository by default:

https://complex256.github.io/mib2q-plugin-sdk/maven

If you are working on the SDK itself, publish the artifacts to a local file repository and point your plugin at it:

# in the SDK checkout
./gradlew publishLocal

# in your plugin project
./gradlew mibPluginJar -Pmibsdk.repo="file:///absolute/path/to/mib2q-plugin-sdk/build/repo"

mibsdk.repo in gradle.properties is the persistent form of the same setting. An empty value means "use the published repository".

docs.title: Optional: Python 3
docs.text: The tutorial's icon generator and the SDK's icon tools are Python 3 scripts with no third-party dependencies. Any image editor that exports 8-bit RGBA PNGs works instead.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: A plugin has two very different halves: Java code that is compiled and backported, and assets that are copied into a package. This page shows where each lives, what ends up on the unit, and where the SDK's own Java/native boundary sits.

docs.title: A plugin project
docs.text:
my-plugin/
├── build.gradle.kts              one plugins block: id("mibsdk.plugin")
├── settings.gradle.kts           the SDK Maven repository
├── gradle.properties             mibsdk.repo and local overrides
├── gradlew, gradlew.bat          the Gradle wrapper
├── gradle/wrapper/               wrapper jar and properties
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/
│   │   │   └── example/myplugin/
│   │   │       └── MyPlugin.java       your code, compiled to v48
│   │   ├── resources/
│   │   │   └── plugin.json             the manifest, copied to the jar root
│   │   └── icons/
│   │       ├── icon.png                72 px Car-row icon (optional)
│   │       └── icon-20.png             20 px status icon (optional)
│   └── test/
│       └── java/example/myplugin/
│           └── MyPluginTest.java       host tests on the real runtime
└── build/                        generated; never edit or commit
Path Kind What it is src/main/java Java Your plugin classes. The build compiles with JDK 17 then lowers them to class-file v48 src/main/resources/plugin.json JSON The manifest. It is copied to the jar root and read by mibpkg and the runtime src/main/icons/<name>.png PNG Icons declared in the manifest. Never copied into the jar src/test/java Java Host tests. Not shipped build.gradle.kts, settings.gradle.kts Kotlin DSL Build configuration. Not shipped gradle/, gradlew* Gradle The wrapper. Not shipped

The layout is fixed by the mibsdk.plugin convention. src/main/resources/plugin.json and src/main/icons/<name>.png are the two paths it requires; everything else is ordinary Gradle.

The install root is written only by mibpkg. The runtime never writes there.

docs.title: 1. Inside your plugin: Java plus assets
docs.text: A plugin package contains only Java class files, plugin.json and PNG icons. There is no native code in a plugin, no .so, no JNI and no NDK. If your plugin needs a native daemon, talk to it over TCP with ctx.net(): loopback by default, outbound with network.outbound.

docs.title: 2. Inside the SDK: Java above, native below
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P["Your plugin<br/>Java, v48 classes"] --> API["mibsdk.api<br/>stable, firmware-neutral"]
    API --> RT["mibsdk.runtime<br/>loader, permissions, scheduler, UI"]
    RT --> SPI["mibsdk.platform<br/>adapter SPI"]
    SPI --> AD["adapter-hqc<br/>the only code that sees stock HMI classes"]
    AD --> STOCK["Stock HMI<br/>lsd.jar, IBM J9 2.3"]
    STOCK --> DSI["DSI services"]
    STOCK --> JNI["JNI: ealswig, jdisplay, ..."]
    DSI --> NATIVE["Native processes<br/>QNX, Kanzi, parking ECU"]
    JNI --> NATIVE
Layer Language Can a plugin see it? Your plugin Java, class-file v48 Yes mibsdk.api Java, v48 Yes mibsdk.runtime, mibsdk.platform Java, v48 No; hidden by the plugin class loader adapter-hqc Java compiled against the stock jars No Stock HMI and DSI Java and JNI No Native QNX services and Kanzi Native No; reachable only through the SDK's API or TCP networking

The plugin class loader exposes only java.*, javax.*, mibsdk.api.*, mibsdk.compat.* and the Retrotranslator runtime. The manufacturer's stock packages and mibsdk.runtime.* are hidden. This is what makes a plugin firmware-neutral: the adapter is the only layer that knows the car.

A plugin cannot patch stock behaviour by shipping classes with the same names. Declarative hooks (ctx.hooks()) are the supported route, and they are limited to parking for now.

docs.title: Test your plugin
docs.text: There is no emulator for the head unit. Host tests use the real SDK runtime on a fake car, so the lifecycle, permissions, UI table, storage and scheduler behave as they do on the unit.

docs.title: The one-line test
docs.text:
@Test
void startsEnabled(@TempDir File tmp) {
    try (PluginTestHarness h = PluginTestHarness.start(tmp)) {
        assertEquals("ENABLED", h.state());
    }
}

PluginTestHarness.start(tmp):

  1. copies the built plugin jar into a temporary "unit" under tmp;
  2. writes sdk.properties with the start delay, heap guard and UI throttle off;
  3. writes grants.properties granting every permission the manifest declares;
  4. installs the icons as mibpkg does, under their content hashes;
  5. starts the runtime and waits until the plugin is ENABLED.

The mibsdk.plugin convention passes -Dmibsdk.pluginJar and -Dmibsdk.pluginIcons to every test, so the harness needs no paths in your code. ./gradlew test builds the jar first and re-runs the tests when the jar or the icons change.

docs.title: Driving the fake unit
docs.text:
Call What it does h.ui() The fake screen (FakeUi) h.car() The fake car (FakePlatform) h.pageKey("timer") A page key: <plugin id>/<page id> h.openPage("timer") Opens a page through the plugin's Plugins-menu link h.advance(ms) Moves the scheduler forward h.await(condition, what) Waits up to 5 s; on failure prints the pages and the runtime log h.state() ENABLED, FAILED, BLOCKED_PERMISSIONS, ... h.log() The runtime log h.storedValues() Stops the runtime, flushes storage and returns it h.restart() Stops and starts on the same directory, keeping storage

FakeUi drivers:

Call Use carRows() The Car drawer, Plugins row first selectRow(i) Selects a Car row render(pageKey) One text line per page entry select(pageKey, itemId) Presses an item or link toggle(pageKey, itemId) Presses a checkbox turn(pageKey, itemId, value) Moves a slider pick(pageKey, itemId, index) Picks a dropdown option choose(pageKey, itemId, index) Opens a choice sub-page and picks an option statusLine(), statusParts(), statusColours(), statusContexts() The status line toast() The current toast dialog(), answer(i), type(text), leave() Confirm and speller openPageKey() The page currently on screen

Every driver does nothing when the entry is not on the page yet or is disabled. After an action that changes the page, await the change before the next one. The plugin's worker updates the UI asynchronously, so an assertion immediately after select can race it.

docs.title: Rendered text
docs.text:
render uses a fixed text format (UiPageText.line):

Entry Rendered as Item Label: value Toggle [on] Label / [off] Label Slider Label: 4 [1..10] Choice / dropdown Label: option Progress Label: 60% Info the text Icon a tag: [png:<sha16>] or [star]

h.iconSha("cup") returns the 16-character hash used in the tag.

docs.title: Grants, features and failures
docs.text:
// No permissions granted: start fails cleanly instead of throwing.
PluginTestHarness h = PluginTestHarness.builder(tmp).grants().startExpectingFailure();
assertEquals("BLOCKED_PERMISSIONS", h.state());

// A unit without native inputs: sliders render as text lines and toasts are inert.
PluginTestHarness h2 = PluginTestHarness.builder(tmp)
        .features(Features.UI_PAGES, Features.SLOT_CAR_MENU)
        .start();

By default the fake unit has every feature and every declared permission.

docs.title: Storage across restarts
docs.text:
Properties before = new Properties();
before.setProperty("minutes", "2");
PluginTestHarness h = PluginTestHarness.builder(tmp).storedValues(before).start();

h.ui().select(h.pageKey("timer"), "start");
h.advance(60_000);
assertEquals("2", h.storedValues().getProperty("minutes"));

storedValues() stops the runtime, so call h.ui() again after h.restart().

docs.title: The fake car
docs.text:
FakePlatform lets you change the unit's state:

h.car().setIgnition(false);                       // publishes IgnitionChanged
h.car().ecuSetSoundDirections(new SoundDirections(true, false, true, true));
h.car().ecuFailWrites(1);                          // next parking write throws
h.car().ecuDropWrites(1);                          // next write is silently lost
h.car().simulateHookCall(HookPoint.PARKING_SOUND_SET, value);

See the Java API reference for the full PluginTestHarness, FakeUi and FakePlatform contracts.

docs.title: What host tests do not cover
docs.text:
• Real HMI rendering, focus and timing.
  • The stock services and DSI behaviour.
  • Native daemons and the real parking ECU.
  • Memory pressure on the 60 MB heap.

Test those on a bench unit, then a car, using Install and debug.

docs.title: Tutorial: build a coffee timer
docs.text:
In this tutorial you will build coffee-timer, a small plugin that:

  • adds a Coffee row with a cup icon to the Car drawer;
  • opens a page with a brew-time slider and a "pop up when ready" toggle;
  • keeps both settings across reboots;
  • counts down on the status line while it brews;
  • shows a toast when the coffee is ready.

The finished plugin is in plugins/coffee-timer. Every marked code block below is compared with that sample by the docs build, so the page and the sample cannot drift apart.

Before you start: install the SDK on the unit and complete Prerequisites. You do not need a unit to write and test the plugin.

docs.title: 1. Create the project
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/complex256/mib2q-plugin-sdk.git
cp -R mib2q-plugin-sdk/templates/plugin coffee-timer
cd coffee-timer

Rename the template's package and class to the tutorial's names:

  • package example.myplugin → tutorial.coffeetimer
  • class MyPlugin → CoffeeTimerPlugin

Delete the scaffolded MyPlugin.java and MyPluginTest.java; you will write the real ones below. Keep the wrapper, the build file and the settings file.

The project should look like this:

coffee-timer/
├── build.gradle.kts
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── gradle.properties
├── gradlew
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/tutorial/coffeetimer/CoffeeTimerPlugin.java
│   │   ├── resources/plugin.json
│   │   └── icons/
│   │       ├── cup.png
│   │       └── cup-20.png
│   └── test/java/tutorial/coffeetimer/CoffeeTimerPluginTest.java
└── .gitignore

docs.title: 2. The manifest
docs.text:
plugin.json tells the build and the unit what the plugin is and what it may do.

{
  "id": "coffee-timer",
  "name": "Coffee Timer",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "your-name",
  "api": 5,
  "main": "tutorial.coffeetimer.CoffeeTimerPlugin",
  "permissions": ["ui.slot.carmenu", "ui.slot.statusbar"],
  "icons": ["cup", "cup-20"]
}
Field Here Why id coffee-timer Names the jar, the package and your storage api 5 The plugin uses a slider and a toast, both api 5 main tutorial.coffeetimer.CoffeeTimerPlugin The class the runtime instantiates permissions ui.slot.carmenu, ui.slot.statusbar One for the Car row, one for the status item and toast icons cup, cup-20 One 72 px row icon and one 20 px status icon

The build validates every name against the permission catalog and fails if your code uses a permission the manifest does not declare.

docs.title: 3. Icons
docs.text:
The sample uses two PNGs:

Icon Size Use cup.png 72×72 Car-drawer row cup-20.png 20×20 Status item and toast

Icons must be 8-bit RGBA (or grey + alpha), non-interlaced, at most 72 px either way and at most 32 KiB. A white glyph on a transparent background looks like the stock icons. The sample's generator is plugins/coffee-timer/make_icons.py:

python3 plugins/coffee-timer/make_icons.py src/main/icons

Any image editor that exports 8-bit RGBA works. The build checks the PNG rules and generates the faded reflection the Car drawer draws under a row icon.

docs.title: 4. The plugin class
docs.text:
Create src/main/java/tutorial/coffeetimer/CoffeeTimerPlugin.java:

package tutorial.coffeetimer;

import mibsdk.api.Icon;
import mibsdk.api.Log;
import mibsdk.api.MibPlugin;
import mibsdk.api.Page;
import mibsdk.api.PageSpec;
import mibsdk.api.PluginContext;
import mibsdk.api.Scheduler;
import mibsdk.api.StatusItem;
import mibsdk.api.Storage;
import mibsdk.api.Subscription;
import mibsdk.api.Ui;
import mibsdk.api.UiAction;

/**
 * A brew timer: a Car-drawer row opens the "Coffee timer" page, where you set the brew time (a slider) and whether a
 * toast pops up when it is done (a toggle). While a timer runs, the status line counts down; when it ends it says
 * "Coffee ready" until you dismiss it. The brew time and the toggle are kept in storage.
 */
public class CoffeeTimerPlugin extends MibPlugin {

    static final String PAGE_ID = "timer";
    static final int MIN_MINUTES = 1;
    static final int MAX_MINUTES = 10;
    static final int DEFAULT_MINUTES = 4;
    static final long MINUTE_MS = 60_000L;

    private Log log;
    private Storage storage;
    private Scheduler scheduler;
    private Ui ui;
    private Page page;
    private StatusItem status;
    private Icon cupSmall;

    private int minutes;           // the brew time, stored as "minutes"
    private boolean toastWhenReady; // stored as "toast" = on|off
    private int left;              // minutes left; 0 when no timer runs
    private boolean ready;         // the timer ended and nobody dismissed it yet
    private Subscription tick;     // the once-a-minute task while a timer runs

    @Override
    protected void onEnable(PluginContext ctx) {
        log = ctx.log();
        storage = ctx.storage();
        scheduler = ctx.scheduler();
        ui = ctx.ui();

        minutes = storedMinutes();
        toastWhenReady = !"off".equals(storage.get("toast", "on"));

        cupSmall = ui.icon("cup-20");
        page = ui.page(spec(), this::onAction);
        ui.carMenuRow("Coffee", page, ui.icon("cup"));
        status = ui.statusItem(null, cupSmall); // hidden until a timer runs
        log.info("enabled, brew time " + minutes + " min");
    }

    @Override
    protected void onDisable() {
        // The runtime has already cancelled the timer, the page, the row and the status item.
        log.info("disabled");
    }

    private void onAction(UiAction a) {
        switch (a.itemId()) {
            case "start" -> start();
            case "stop" -> stop();
            case "dismiss" -> {
                ready = false;
                status.set(null);
            }
            case "toast" -> {
                toastWhenReady = a.requestedOn().booleanValue();
                storage.put("toast", toastWhenReady ? "on" : "off");
            }
            case "minutes" -> {
                minutes = a.value().intValue();
                storage.put("minutes", String.valueOf(minutes));
            }
            default -> log.warn("unknown item " + a.itemId());
        }
        page.update(spec());
    }

    private void start() {
        cancelTick();
        ready = false;
        left = minutes;
        tick = scheduler.every(MINUTE_MS, this::onMinute);
        status.set("Coffee " + left + "m", cupSmall);
        log.info("brewing for " + minutes + " min");
    }

    private void stop() {
        cancelTick();
        left = 0;
        status.set(null);
        log.info("stopped");
    }

    private void onMinute() {
        left--;
        if (left > 0) {
            status.set("Coffee " + left + "m", cupSmall);
        } else {
            cancelTick();
            ready = true;
            status.set("Coffee ready", cupSmall);
            if (toastWhenReady) {
                ui.toast("Coffee is ready", cupSmall);
            }
            log.info("ready");
        }
        page.update(spec());
    }

    private void cancelTick() {
        if (tick != null) {
            tick.cancel();
            tick = null;
        }
    }

    private PageSpec spec() {
        PageSpec s = PageSpec.of(PAGE_ID, "Coffee timer");
        s = left > 0 ? s.item("stop", "Stop timer", left + " min left") : s.item("start", "Start timer", minutes + " min");
        if (ready) {
            s = s.item("dismiss", "Dismiss", null);
        }
        return s.toggle("toast", "Pop up when ready", toastWhenReady)
                .slider("minutes", "Brew time", MIN_MINUTES, MAX_MINUTES, 1, minutes, false)
                .info(ready ? "Your coffee is ready." : left > 0 ? "Brewing..." : "Set a brew time, then Start.");
    }

    /** The stored brew time, or the default when none is stored or it is out of range. */
    private int storedMinutes() {
        try {
            int m = Integer.parseInt(storage.get("minutes", String.valueOf(DEFAULT_MINUTES)));
            return m >= MIN_MINUTES && m <= MAX_MINUTES ? m : DEFAULT_MINUTES;
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return DEFAULT_MINUTES;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: What each part does
docs.text:
Lifecycle. The runtime creates the class with its no-argument constructor and calls onEnable(ctx) once, on the plugin's own worker thread. PluginContext is the only door to the SDK. When the plugin is disabled, reloaded, quarantined or the HMI shuts down, the runtime cancels everything the plugin registered and then calls onDisable(). You do not have to clean up.

onDisable() also runs after an onEnable() that threw. Keep it defensive: fields assigned after the failure point are still null.

One worker per plugin. onEnable, page actions, scheduler tasks, event listeners and dialog answers all run on one SDK-owned thread, one at a time. That is why this class needs no synchronized and no volatile. It also means a slow callback blocks the rest of your plugin: the SDK logs calls over 5 s and quarantines a call that runs for 30 s. Your code never runs on an HMI thread.

A page and a Car row.

page = ui.page(spec(), this::onAction);
ui.carMenuRow("Coffee", page, ui.icon("cup"));

ui.page registers the page; the SDK also lists it under the plugin's entry in the Plugins menu. carMenuRow adds the Car-drawer row. A plugin may have at most 8 pages and 2 Car rows.

PageSpec is immutable. Every builder call returns a new spec; to change the screen, build a new spec and call page.update(spec). spec() rebuilds the page from the plugin's fields, which is the pattern the samples use.

A toggle and a slider.

return s.toggle("toast", "Pop up when ready", toastWhenReady)
        .slider("minutes", "Brew time", MIN_MINUTES, MAX_MINUTES, 1, minutes, false)
        .info(...);

A toggle is the HMI's native checkbox. It does not flip by itself: you receive requestedOn() and must store the value and update the page. A slider sends each knob step as value(). It shows its position, not its number, so the "Start timer" row shows the minutes in its value column.

A page may have at most 4 slider plus dropdown rows; they are drawn after the list rows. Slider rules: min < max, (max - min) % step == 0, at most 24 steps, and the current value on the grid.

A status item.

status = ui.statusItem(null, cupSmall);
status.set("Coffee " + left + "m", cupSmall);

A plugin has one status item. set(null) or set("") hides it. Text is capped at 12 characters; the line is shared with other plugins and the SDK's own indicators, so put the important part first. set never fails because the user hid the item.

A toast.

ui.toast("Coffee is ready", cupSmall);

A toast shows 20 characters and an optional 20 px icon for 3 seconds. It needs ui.slot.statusbar and is inert if the unit cannot show inputs.

Storage. storage.get/put/remove is a string map per plugin, persisted across reboots. It is capped at 256 KiB per plugin and 1 MiB for all plugins; a put past the cap throws. Parse stored values defensively, as storedMinutes() does, because the data may come from an older version of your plugin.

Missing features are not errors. If the unit cannot show the UI this boot, page, carMenuRow, statusItem and toast still return handles, but they are inert. Count and argument checks still apply. Use ctx.has(Features.SLOT_CAR_MENU) and friends when you need to know.

docs.title: 5. Run it on your computer
docs.text:
There is no emulator for the head unit. Instead, PluginTestHarness installs the built jar into a temporary "unit", starts the real runtime on a fake car and gives you a fake screen.

Create src/test/java/tutorial/coffeetimer/CoffeeTimerPluginTest.java:

package tutorial.coffeetimer;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNull;

import java.io.File;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Properties;
import mibsdk.adapter.fake.FakeUi;
import mibsdk.test.PluginTestHarness;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.io.TempDir;

class CoffeeTimerPluginTest {

    @TempDir
    File tmp;

    private PluginTestHarness h;
    /** What the plugin stored on an earlier run: set before start. */
    private final Properties stored = new Properties();
    private FakeUi ui;
    /** A plugin page's key is "<plugin id>/<page id>". */
    private String page;
    private String row;
    private String cup20Sha;

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        if (h != null) {
            h.close();
        }
    }

    /** Installs the built jar into a temp "unit", starts the real runtime on the fake car and waits for the page. */
    private void start() {
        h = PluginTestHarness.builder(tmp).storedValues(stored).start();
        ui = h.ui();
        page = h.pageKey("timer");
        row = "[png:" + h.iconSha("cup") + "] Coffee";
        cup20Sha = h.iconSha("cup-20");
        h.await(() -> !ui.render(page).isEmpty(), "the page");
    }

    private void minutePasses() {
        h.advance(CoffeeTimerPlugin.MINUTE_MS);
    }

    // ---- the tests ----

    @Test
    void carRowOpensTheTimerPage() {
        start();
        h.await(() -> ui.carRows().contains(row), "the Coffee row: " + ui.carRows());
        ui.selectRow(ui.carRows().indexOf(row));
        h.await(() -> page.equals(ui.openPageKey()), "the page open");
        assertEquals(Arrays.asList(
                "Start timer: 4 min",
                "[on] Pop up when ready",
                "Brew time: 4 [1..10]",
                "Set a brew time, then Start."), ui.render(page));
    }

    @Test
    void sliderAndToggleAreStored() {
        start();
        ui.turn(page, "minutes", 7);
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Start timer: 7 min"), "7 min");
        ui.toggle(page, "toast");
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("[off] Pop up when ready"), "toggle off");
        Properties stored = h.storedValues();
        assertEquals("7", stored.getProperty("minutes"));
        assertEquals("off", stored.getProperty("toast"));
    }

    @Test
    void storedValuesAreRestored() {
        stored.setProperty("minutes", "2");
        stored.setProperty("toast", "off");
        start();
        List<String> lines = ui.render(page);
        assertEquals("Start timer: 2 min", lines.get(0));
        assertEquals("[off] Pop up when ready", lines.get(1));
    }

    @Test
    void timerCountsDownOnTheStatusLineAndToasts() {
        start();
        ui.turn(page, "minutes", 2);
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Start timer: 2 min"), "2 min");
        assertEquals("", ui.statusLine());
        ui.select(page, "start");
        h.await(() -> "Coffee 2m".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee 2m on the status line");
        minutePasses();
        h.await(() -> "Coffee 1m".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee 1m");
        assertNull(ui.toast());
        minutePasses();
        h.await(() -> "Coffee ready".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee ready");
        h.await(() -> ("[png:" + cup20Sha + "] Coffee is ready").equals(ui.toast()), "the toast: " + ui.toast());
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Dismiss"), "the Dismiss row");
        ui.select(page, "dismiss");
        h.await(() -> "".equals(ui.statusLine()), "the status item hidden");
    }

    @Test
    void noToastWhenTurnedOff() {
        start();
        ui.toggle(page, "toast");
        ui.turn(page, "minutes", 1);
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Start timer: 1 min"), "1 min");
        ui.select(page, "start");
        h.await(() -> "Coffee 1m".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee 1m");
        minutePasses();
        h.await(() -> "Coffee ready".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee ready");
        assertNull(ui.toast());
    }

    @Test
    void stopCancelsTheTimer() {
        start();
        ui.select(page, "start");
        h.await(() -> "Coffee 4m".equals(ui.statusLine()), "Coffee 4m");
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Stop timer: 4 min left"), "the Stop row");
        ui.select(page, "stop");
        h.await(() -> ui.render(page).contains("Start timer: 4 min"), "back to Start");
        assertEquals("", ui.statusLine());
    }
}

Run it:

./gradlew test

The build passes the jar and the icons to the test. h.await(...) waits up to five seconds for the runtime, so assertions are not racing the plugin's worker thread. h.advance(ms) moves the plugin's scheduler forward, so a two-minute timer runs in milliseconds.

See Test your plugin for the rest of the harness API.

docs.title: 6. Build the jar
docs.text:
./gradlew mibPluginJar

Output:

build/mibsdk/coffee-timer.jar
build/mibsdk/coffee-timer.jar.stamp
build/reports/mibsdk/linkcheck.txt
build/reports/mibsdk/permissions.txt

Do not edit the jar after the build: mibpkg checks the stamp, which records the checks and the jar's SHA-256.

docs.title: 7. Package and install
docs.text:
./gradlew mibpkgPackage -Pmibsdk.mibpkg=/path/to/mibpkg

Output: build/mibsdk/coffee-timer-1.0.0.mpk.

Install it with the mibpkg web interface, or over SSH:

installer/mibsdk-dev install-plugin build/mibsdk/coffee-timer-1.0.0.mpk <unit-ip>
# exits 3 and lists the permissions:
installer/mibsdk-dev install-plugin build/mibsdk/coffee-timer-1.0.0.mpk \
    --approve=ui.slot.carmenu,ui.slot.statusbar <unit-ip>

Open the Car drawer. The Coffee row is there.

docs.title: The fast loop
docs.text:
Once the package is installed (so the grants and icons exist on the unit), push code changes as a jar:

./gradlew mibPluginJar
installer/mibsdk-dev push build/mibsdk/coffee-timer.jar <unit-ip>

The runtime hot-reloads the jar within a couple of seconds, with no HMI restart. A push carries only the jar: new icons or new permissions need a new package.
